m1.q: A customer's UPI payment shows as received by the shop within two seconds. What has definitely happened at that moment?
o: The two banks have settled with each other at the RBI
The payment message has cleared and the shop's bank has credited the shop
The RBI has debited the payer's bank
Nothing — the credit is provisional until end of day
m1.x: Instant rails clear the message and credit the payee immediately; interbank settlement between the two banks happens later in net cycles at the central bank.

m1.q: Which statement about clearing and settlement is correct?
o: Clearing moves the money; settlement exchanges the information
Clearing exchanges the information and works out who owes whom; settlement moves the money
They are two words for the same step
m1.x: Clearing is the exchange and reconciliation of payment instructions; settlement is the final transfer of funds between banks, usually across central-bank accounts.

m1.q: Why does a cheque take one to two days when a UPI transfer takes seconds?
o: Cheques are paper, so they are slower to type in
Cheques are cleared in batches and settled on a net basis at the end of a cycle, plus physical presentation and fraud checks
Banks charge more for UPI so they prioritise it
m1.x: Cheque clearing is a deferred net system with presentation cycles; UPI clears each message in real time and credits ahead of settlement.

m1.q: Which is an example of a gross settlement system?
m1.x: RTGS settles each payment individually and finally in real time. NEFT, cheques and card schemes settle net positions in cycles.

m2.q: Which Indian system is operated directly by the RBI rather than by NPCI?
m2.x: RTGS and NEFT are owned and operated by the RBI. UPI, IMPS, AEPS and BBPS are NPCI products.

m2.q: NEFT is electronic, yet it is not instant. Why?
o: It runs only during banking hours
It settles in half-hourly batches on a net basis
It needs manual approval at the RBI
m2.x: NEFT collects instructions and settles them in half-hourly batches, 24x7. IMPS and UPI clear each message in real time.

m2.q: What does the ₹2 lakh minimum on RTGS achieve?
o: It stops small customers from using banks' systems
It pushes high-value, high-risk payments onto a gross, final settlement rail and leaves small payments to cheaper netted systems
m2.x: Large payments carry the most settlement risk, so the design steers them to RTGS where there is no interbank exposure.

m2.q: A UPI 'collect' request arrives on your phone. What kind of payment is it structurally?
o: A pure pull — money leaves when the merchant asks
A pull request that becomes a push only when you authorise it with your PIN
A direct debit under a mandate
m2.x: Your bank debits you only after you approve. That design is why UPI collect is safer than an open pull, and why NPCI has restricted collect requests from unknown parties.

m3.q: What does Swift actually move between banks?
m3.x: Swift carries secure, guaranteed-delivery messages. The money moves afterwards through nostro/vostro and central-bank accounts because the message instructed it.

o: A 36-character reference generated by the first bank and copied unchanged into every message about that payment
The Swift code of the beneficiary bank
m3.x: The Unique End-to-end Transaction Reference ties the whole chain together and is what the gpi Tracker uses.

m3.q: Since November 2018, what happens to a cross-border payment instruction sent without a UETR?
o: It is delivered with a warning
It is rejected by the network (NAK)
It is charged a higher fee
m3.x: Swift mandated UETRs for all payment instructions from SR2018; non-compliant messages receive a NAK.

o: A new payment network replacing correspondent banking
A service-level rulebook plus a central Tracker on top of the existing network
The name for ISO 20022 on Swift
m3.x: gpi adds rules (speed, fee transparency, tracking, unaltered remittance data) and the Tracker; it does not change how money settles.

m4.q: Bank X in Mumbai holds a USD account with Citi New York. From Bank X's books, what is that account?
m4.x: 'Our account with you' is a nostro, and it is money Bank X owns, so it is an asset on Bank X's balance sheet.

m4.q: The same account, seen from Citi's books, is…
o: A vostro — a liability, because Citi owes Bank X that money
m4.x: One account, two names: nostro for the owner, vostro for the holder. For Citi it is a deposit it owes to Bank X.

m4.q: What is a nostro mirror account?
o: Citi's copy of Bank X's statement
Bank X's own internal record of what its nostro balance at Citi should be
A second nostro at another bank
m4.x: Bank X cannot see Citi's ledger in real time, so it keeps its own mirror; reconciling the mirror against Citi's MT940/camt.053 statement is a core daily task.

m4.q: In a payment chain, what is the 'account with institution'?
o: The bank that holds the beneficiary's account (the creditor agent)
m4.x: 'Account with institution' is the older MT term (field 57) for the bank where the beneficiary's account is held — creditor agent in ISO 20022.

o: Deutsche Bank, Denmark, Frankfurt, head office
Deutsche Bank, Germany, branch FF, location 500
m5.x: DEUT = institution, DE = Germany, FF = Frankfurt, 500 = branch code.

m5.q: A €10,000 payment passes two intermediaries charging €15 each and a beneficiary bank charging €10, under SHA. The beneficiary receives…
m5.x: Under SHA the payer covers only their own bank's fee; intermediaries and the beneficiary bank deduct theirs: 10,000 − 15 − 15 − 10 = 9,960.

m5.q: A payer chooses OUR, yet the beneficiary still receives less than the full amount. The most likely reason is…
o: OUR is not valid for euro payments
An intermediary deducted a fee because it had no agreement to bill the sending bank
The beneficiary bank ignored the message
The payer's bank converted it to BEN
m5.x: OUR is an instruction, not a guarantee; a bank in the chain that will not bill back may still deduct. gpi fee transparency exists to show where.

m5.q: What does a NAK from Swift mean?
o: The network refused the message, for example a validation failure or a missing UETR, so it never reached the receiver
The payment was returned after settlement
The message was delivered but not read
m5.x: ACK/NAK are network-level acknowledgements of the message, not business responses to the payment.

m6.q: In the cover method, which message goes directly from the payer's bank to the beneficiary's bank?
m6.x: The customer transfer (pacs.008) is the announcement sent straight to the beneficiary bank; the cover (pacs.009 COV) moves the money through the correspondents.

m6.q: In the serial method, which banks see the payer's and beneficiary's full details?
o: Only the first and last banks
Every bank in the chain, because each forwards a customer transfer
m6.x: Serial payments pass the pacs.008/MT103 hop by hop, so each bank processes and can screen the full customer data.

m6.q: Why was MT202 COV introduced in 2009?
o: So the cover leg carries originator and beneficiary details for sanctions screening, instead of only bank names
m6.x: Plain MT202 covers hid the underlying customers from intermediaries; regulators required the COV variant to carry them.

m6.q: What must the beneficiary's bank do before crediting the customer in a cover payment?
o: Match the incoming cover credit against the announcement it received, then credit
m6.x: Announcement without cover, or cover without announcement, is a classic investigations case; the bank credits only when both match.

m7.q: Which MT message is the customer credit transfer, and what replaced it in ISO 20022?
m7.x: MT103 is the single customer credit transfer; its ISO 20022 equivalent is pacs.008. MT202 maps to pacs.009, MT101 to pain.001, MT940 to camt.053.

m7.q: What is the difference between MT940 and MT942?
o: MT940 is for corporates, MT942 for banks
MT940 is the end-of-day statement; MT942 is an intraday report of entries booked since the last one
MT942 includes balances, MT940 does not
m7.x: MT942 entries are preliminary notifications during the day; MT940 is the definitive end-of-day statement with opening and closing balances.

o: Confirmation of debit and confirmation of credit, sent by an account-servicing bank to the account owner
m7.x: MT900 confirms a debit, MT910 a credit; both map to camt.054 in ISO 20022.

o: The charge-bearer code: OUR, SHA or BEN
m7.x: 71A is 'Details of charges'. Field 59 is the beneficiary, 32A the value date and amount, 70 the remittance information.

m8.q: Which ISO 20022 family travels on the interbank (bank-to-bank) edge of the four-corner model?
m8.x: pain is customer-to-bank initiation, pacs is bank-to-bank clearing and settlement, camt is cash-management reporting and investigations.

o: The MT/MX coexistence period for cross-border payment instructions ended; pacs messages became mandatory for CBPR+ traffic
m8.x: Payment instructions (MT103/202 family) migrated fully; statements, investigations and other families follow through 2026–2028.

m8.q: Which is an example of the 'richer data' ISO 20022 brings?
o: Separate elements for street, town, postcode and country, plus coded purpose and structured remittance
m8.x: Structured fields are what make screening more precise and reconciliation automatable — and what causes truncation problems when converted back to MT.

m8.q: What changes in November 2026 for CBPR+ and SEPA messages?
o: Unstructured postal addresses are no longer permitted; addresses must be structured or hybrid
m8.x: The one-year grace period for unstructured addresses ends in November 2026; expect rejects from counterparties that still send free text.

m9.q: A payment is accepted and settled, then sent back two days later because the account is closed. This is a…
m9.x: After settlement, money coming back is a return (pacs.004). Before settlement it would be a reject (pacs.002). A recall is the payer asking for money back.

m9.q: What is the key difference between a reject and a return?
o: Rejects are for direct debits only
In a reject no money moved, so nothing comes back; in a return money moved and is sent back as a new payment
Rejects need a reason code, returns do not
m9.x: Both carry ISO reason codes; the difference is whether settlement had already happened.
AC04 = closed account. AM04 = insufficient funds, MD01 = no mandate, RC01 = bank identifier incorrect.

m9.q: Under SEPA, a payer who typed the wrong IBAN and wants the money back initiates a…
o: Recall (camt.056), which the beneficiary's bank puts to its customer
m9.x: Credit transfers have no refund right; the payer's bank sends a recall request and the beneficiary must agree.

m10.q: Which ISO 20022 message replaces MT192 (request for cancellation)?
m10.x: camt.056 is the FI-to-FI payment cancellation request; camt.029 is the response (replacing MT196).

o: The beneficiary bank received funds but cannot credit them, for example because the account number does not match
m10.x: Unable to apply (camt.026 in the older set) is raised by the receiving bank when it cannot process a credit it has received.

o: The payer's bank, on behalf of a payer whose beneficiary says the money never arrived
m10.x: The payer side asks where the money is; the chain responds with resolution of investigation (camt.029).

m10.q: From November 2027, how do cross-border investigations have to be exchanged?
o: Only as ISO 20022 camt.110/camt.111 through Swift Case Management; MT192/195/196 are retired
m10.x: Cancellations move to Stop and Recall / Case Management from November 2026; the legacy MT investigation messages end in November 2027.

o: A payment processed in a straight line between two branches
A payment that completes end to end with no manual intervention
m11.x: STP rate is the share of payments that never land in a repair or exception queue. It is the headline efficiency metric of a payments operation.

m11.q: Which is NOT a typical reason a payment drops out of STP into a repair queue?
o: Missing purpose code required by the destination country
m11.x: Currency alone does not cause repair; invalid identifiers, screening hits, missing mandatory data and cut-off issues do.

o: A customer logs in to internet banking
A corporate's ERP exchanges payment files and statements with the bank directly over a secure channel such as SFTP, without a portal
Two banks sharing a data centre
m11.x: H2H is file-based, automated and encrypted; APIs are the newer alternative for the same job.

m11.q: What is the difference between a payment engine and a payment hub?
o: An engine processes one rail or product; a hub orchestrates many channels, rails and formats through shared validation, screening, routing and exception handling
An engine is for cards only
m11.x: Hubs consolidate what used to be separate engines so rules, screening and reporting are applied once.

m12.q: 'Outbound cross-border payments must carry a structured beneficiary address by November 2026 to avoid rejects' is a…
m12.x: It states the business need and outcome. The functional requirement would specify what the system must do (validate fields, block or warn, which messages).

m12.q: In Scrum, who owns and orders the product backlog?
m12.x: The Product Owner is accountable for the backlog; the Scrum Master serves the team and the process; developers own the sprint backlog.

m12.q: Which testing level checks that the whole system meets business needs, usually with business users?
m12.x: UAT is where a payments BA spends much of their time: writing scenarios, preparing test data such as sample pacs.008 messages, and getting sign-off.

m12.q: Which SQL query returns the number of returned payments per reason code last month?
o: SELECT reason_code FROM payments WHERE status = 'RETURNED'
SELECT reason_code, COUNT(*) FROM payments WHERE status = 'RETURNED' AND value_date >= '2026-09-01' AND value_date < '2026-10-01' GROUP BY reason_code
SELECT * FROM payments GROUP BY reason_code
m12.x: You need a filter on status and date, a COUNT, and a GROUP BY on the reason code.
